title: Open channel flow
summary: Manning's equation and the specific energy curve carry this subchapter. The single most valuable idea is the Froude number: Fr < 1 subcritical, = 1 critical, > 1 supercritical — because it determines which end of a channel controls the flow, whether a hydraulic jump can form, and which surface profile develops. Learn the most economical sections (rectangle b = 2y, trapezoid with an inscribed semicircle) and the jump relations, and most questions follow.

sections.heading: Uniform flow and the resistance equations
sections.body:
**Open channel flow** has a **free surface at atmospheric pressure**, so **gravity drives it** and the Froude number governs — unlike pipe flow, where pressure drives and Reynolds governs.

**Geometric elements:**

| Element | Meaning |
|---|---|
| **Wetted perimeter P** | Length of the boundary **in contact with water** — the free surface is **not** included |
| **Hydraulic radius R** | **A / P** |
| Hydraulic depth | A / T (T = top width) |
| Section factor | A√D |

**Chézy's equation:**

> **V = C √(R S)**

**Manning's equation** — the practical standard:

> **V = (1/n) R^{2/3} S^{1/2}**,  and  **Q = (1/n) A R^{2/3} S^{1/2}**

with **C = R^{1/6}/n** linking the two.

**Manning's n** by surface:

| Surface | n |
|---|---|
| **Smooth cement plaster / finished concrete** | **0.011 – 0.013** |
| Rough concrete, brickwork | 0.015 – 0.017 |
| **Earth channel, clean** | **0.020 – 0.025** |
| Earth channel, weedy or stony | 0.030 – 0.040 |
| **Natural stream, clean and straight** | **0.030** |
| Natural stream, sluggish with pools and weeds | 0.050 – 0.100 |
| Mountain stream with boulders | 0.040 – 0.070 |

Note that n is **not** dimensionless and carries units of s/m^{1/3}, which is why Manning's equation looks different in imperial units (a factor of 1.486). Its great practical merit is that n depends **almost entirely on the surface** and hardly at all on the depth or the Reynolds number, so a single tabulated value serves over a wide range.

**A wide rectangular channel** gives a useful simplification worth spotting immediately:

> If **b ≫ y**, then **P ≈ b** and **R = by/(b + 2y) → y**

So **R ≈ y** for a wide channel, which reduces Manning's equation to **V = (1/n) y^{2/3} S^{1/2}** and makes many problems tractable by hand.

**Normal depth y_n** is the depth of **uniform flow** for a given Q, S and n — found by trial from Manning's equation, since it appears in both A and R. It is the depth the flow would reach if the channel were long enough at constant slope.

**Most economical (efficient) section.** For a given area, the section with the **minimum wetted perimeter** gives the maximum discharge — because R = A/P is then largest.

| Section | Condition for efficiency |
|---|---|
| **Rectangle** | **b = 2y** (width = twice depth), so **R = y/2** |
| **Trapezoid** | The **sloping side equals the half top width**, and an **inscribed semicircle** of radius y touches all three sides; **R = y/2** |
| **Triangle** | Vertex angle 90° |
| **Circle (part full)** | Maximum Q at **y = 0.94 D**; maximum V at **y = 0.81 D** |
| **Semicircle** | The **most efficient of all** sections |

The semicircle is most efficient because a circle encloses the greatest area for a given perimeter. It is rarely built because it is difficult to construct and maintain — so the **trapezoid** with its inscribed semicircle is the practical compromise, and is the standard canal shape.

The **part-full circular pipe** results are worth noting: **both maximum discharge and maximum velocity occur before the pipe is full**. Near the crown, the added wetted perimeter costs more than the added area gains, so a sewer running absolutely full is **less** efficient than one running nearly full — the basis of the hydraulic elements diagram used in sewer design.

sections.heading: Specific energy, critical flow and the Froude number
sections.body:
**Specific energy** is the energy per unit weight measured **from the channel bed**:

> **E = y + V²/2g = y + Q²/(2gA²)**

Plotting E against y for constant Q gives the **specific energy curve**, whose shape carries most of the theory:

- It has **two limbs** and a **minimum**.
- For any **E greater than E_min** there are **two possible depths** — the **alternate depths**, one subcritical (large y, small V) and one supercritical (small y, large V).
- At **E_min** the two coincide at the **critical depth y_c**.
- **No flow is possible for E < E_min.**

**At the critical depth**, differentiating E with respect to y gives the general condition

> **Q² T / (g A³) = 1**,  equivalently  **Fr = 1**

For a **rectangular** channel this reduces to the two results worth memorising:

> **y_c = (q²/g)^{1/3}**  (q = Q/b, discharge per unit width)
> **E_min = 1.5 y_c**,  and  **V_c = √(g y_c)**

**The Froude number:**

> **Fr = V / √(g y)**

| Fr | Regime | Depth & velocity | Control |
|---|---|---|---|
| **< 1** | **Subcritical (tranquil)** | Deep, slow | **Downstream** control — disturbances travel **upstream** |
| **= 1** | **Critical** | y = y_c | — |
| **> 1** | **Supercritical (rapid)** | Shallow, fast | **Upstream** control — disturbances **cannot** travel upstream |

**The physical meaning of Fr = 1** is the key: **√(gy) is the speed of a small surface wave** in shallow water. So Fr is the ratio of flow speed to wave speed. When Fr < 1 a wave can outrun the flow and travel upstream, so downstream conditions influence the upstream flow. When Fr > 1 it cannot, so the flow is oblivious to what lies downstream.

That single fact explains a great deal:

- Why a **gate or weir downstream controls** a subcritical reach but not a supercritical one.
- Why a **hydraulic jump can only form** where flow passes from supercritical to subcritical — the flow must be forced to become aware of downstream conditions, and it does so abruptly.
- Why computation of a surface profile proceeds **upstream** in subcritical flow and **downstream** in supercritical flow.

**Critical slope** is the bed slope at which uniform flow occurs at the critical depth. Comparing y_n with y_c classifies the channel:

| Channel | Condition |
|---|---|
| **Mild (M)** | **y_n > y_c** |
| **Critical (C)** | y_n = y_c |
| **Steep (S)** | **y_n < y_c** |
| Horizontal (H) | S = 0, y_n infinite |
| Adverse (A) | Negative slope |

**A channel is mild or steep by comparison of depths, not by the numerical value of the slope** — the same slope can be mild for one discharge and steep for another, since y_n depends on Q. This is a frequently examined subtlety.

**Applications of specific energy:** flow over a **hump** (the depth falls in subcritical flow and rises in supercritical flow — counter-intuitive but a direct consequence of the E–y curve), flow through a **contraction**, and the **broad-crested weir**, where critical depth occurs on the crest and gives a unique relation between head and discharge — which is why such weirs make good flow-measuring structures.

sections.heading: The hydraulic jump
sections.body:
A **hydraulic jump** is the abrupt transition from **supercritical to subcritical** flow, accompanied by a great deal of turbulence and **energy loss**. It is the one common flow feature where Bernoulli fails outright and the **momentum equation** must be used, because the loss is unknown in advance.

**The sequent (conjugate) depth relation**, from momentum:

> **y₂/y₁ = ½ (√(1 + 8 Fr₁²) − 1)**

Note these are **sequent** depths — related by momentum — and are quite different from the **alternate** depths related by energy. Confusing the two is a standard error.

**Energy loss:**

> **E_L = (y₂ − y₁)³ / (4 y₁ y₂)**

**Length of jump ≈ 5 to 7 y₂**, and the **height of the jump** is y₂ − y₁.

**Classification by the upstream Froude number:**

| Fr₁ | Type | Character |
|---|---|---|
| 1.0 – 1.7 | **Undular** | Standing waves; very little loss |
| 1.7 – 2.5 | **Weak** | Smooth rise; loss ~5–15% |
| 2.5 – 4.5 | **Oscillating** | Unstable jet; **generates waves that travel downstream** — to be avoided |
| **4.5 – 9.0** | **Steady** | **Well-established, stable — the best for a stilling basin** |
| > 9.0 | **Strong** | Very rough; loss up to 85% but severe scour risk |

The **oscillating** range 2.5–4.5 is deliberately avoided in design because the wave train it sends downstream erodes banks for a long distance. The **steady** range 4.5–9.0 is the design target.

**Why the jump is deliberately created.** Downstream of a **spillway, sluice gate or canal fall**, the water arrives with a very high velocity that would scour the channel bed. A jump **dissipates that energy in a controlled position** — inside a concrete **stilling basin** — rather than allowing it to be dissipated by eroding the river.

**The design requirement** is that the **tailwater level must match the sequent depth y₂**. If the tailwater is too low the jump sweeps downstream out of the basin, and scour occurs beyond the protected length; if too high the jump is **submerged** and dissipates less energy. Matching them is achieved by setting the basin floor level, or by an **end sill, chute blocks and baffle blocks** (USBR basin types II to IV, selected by Fr₁).

**Other uses of a jump:** mixing chemicals in water treatment, aerating water, and as a **flow measuring** device.

**Surges and waves.** A **surge** is a moving hydraulic jump, produced by a sudden gate operation. **Positive** surges (increasing depth) are stable and steepen; **negative** surges (decreasing depth) flatten as they travel, because the wave celerity depends on depth. This is why a sudden gate closure sends a steep-fronted wave upstream while a sudden opening sends a gentle drawdown.

sections.heading: Gradually varied flow and flow measurement
sections.body:
**Gradually varied flow (GVF)** is steady non-uniform flow in which the depth changes **slowly** along the channel, so the pressure remains hydrostatic and friction can be computed from Manning's equation using the local depth.

> **dy/dx = (S_0 − S_f) / (1 − Fr²)**

The **dynamic equation of GVF**, and the whole classification of surface profiles follows from the **signs of its numerator and denominator**:

| Numerator (S_0 − S_f) | Denominator (1 − Fr²) | dy/dx |
|---|---|---|
| + | + (subcritical) | **Rising** — backwater |
| − | + | **Falling** — drawdown |
| + | − (supercritical) | Falling |
| − | − | Rising |

Note that **dy/dx → ∞ when Fr → 1**: the equation breaks down at critical depth, which is exactly why the transition through critical is **abrupt** (a jump or a free overfall) rather than gradual.

**The thirteen profiles** are named by channel type and by which of the three zones the depth lies in:

| Profile | Channel | Depth zone | Example |
|---|---|---|---|
| **M1** | Mild | y > y_n > y_c | **Backwater curve behind a dam or weir** |
| **M2** | Mild | y_n > y > y_c | **Drawdown to a free overfall** |
| M3 | Mild | y_n > y_c > y | Downstream of a sluice gate on a mild slope |
| **S1** | Steep | y > y_c > y_n | Behind an obstruction on a steep slope |
| S2 | Steep | y_c > y > y_n | Downstream of a break in grade to steep |
| S3 | Steep | y_c > y_n > y | Downstream of a gate on a steep slope |
| H2, H3 | Horizontal | — | — |
| A2, A3 | Adverse | — | — |
| C1, C3 | Critical | — | — |

**M1 and M2 are the two to know by name.** The **M1 backwater curve** is what determines how far upstream a dam or a bridge raises the water level — hence the extent of **submergence and the height of marginal embankments**. The **M2 drawdown** occurs approaching a free overfall or a steepening.

**Computation** of a GVF profile proceeds by the **direct step** method (compute x for chosen y) or the **standard step** method (compute y at chosen x, needed where the section varies), integrating from a **control section** — and **upstream** for subcritical flow, **downstream** for supercritical, following the direction of control.

**Rapidly varied flow (RVF)** is the opposite case: depth changes abruptly over a short distance, so friction is negligible but the pressure is not hydrostatic. The **hydraulic jump**, flow over a **weir** and through a **sluice gate** are the standard cases.

**Weirs and notches** — the exponents are the examinable part:

| Type | Discharge | Exponent |
|---|---|---|
| **Rectangular** | Q = (2/3) C_d L √(2g) H^{3/2} | **H^{3/2}** |
| **Triangular (V-notch)** | Q = (8/15) C_d √(2g) tan(θ/2) H^{5/2} | **H^{5/2}** |
| Trapezoidal (Cipolletti) | Sum of the two | — |
| **Broad-crested weir** | Q = 1.705 C_d L H^{3/2} | H^{3/2} |
| **Ogee (spillway)** | Q = C L H^{3/2}, C ≈ 2.2 | H^{3/2} |

**The V-notch is more accurate at low flows** than a rectangular weir, precisely because its area shrinks with head — so a small change in discharge produces a relatively large change in head, which is easier to measure. That is why V-notches are used for gauging small streams and laboratory flows.

**Note that all rectangular-type weirs give Q ∝ H^{3/2}**, whether sharp-crested, broad-crested or ogee — only the coefficient differs. A question offering **√H** as an option for a weir is offering an impossible exponent.

**Corrections** in weir measurement: **velocity of approach** (add the approach velocity head to H), **end contractions** (reduce the effective length), and **Francis's formula** for the standard rectangular case.

**Other measuring structures:** the **venturi flume** and **standing wave flume**, which create critical flow in a contraction and so give a unique head–discharge relation without a drop in bed level — valuable in an irrigation canal where a weir's head loss cannot be afforded.

**Velocity measurement in a natural channel** uses a **current meter** at 0.6 depth (or the mean of 0.2 and 0.8 depth) across several verticals, the discharge being the sum of segment areas times their mean velocities — the **velocity–area** method, and the basis of every river gauging station.

formulas.label: Manning and Chézy
formulas.note: For a wide rectangular channel R ≈ y. n ≈ 0.011 smooth concrete, 0.025 clean earth channel.

formulas.label: Most economical sections
formulas.expression: Rectangle b = 2y (R = y/2);  Trapezoid: inscribed semicircle of radius y (R = y/2);  Semicircle most efficient of all
formulas.note: Minimum wetted perimeter for a given area. Part-full circle: max Q at 0.94D, max V at 0.81D.

formulas.label: Specific energy and critical depth
formulas.expression: E = y + Q²/(2gA²) ;   critical: Q²T/(gA³) = 1 ;   rectangular: y_c = (q²/g)^{1/3}, E_min = 1.5 y_c
formulas.note: Two alternate depths exist for any E above E_min; no flow is possible below it.

formulas.label: Froude number
formulas.expression: Fr = V/√(gy) — <1 subcritical (downstream control), =1 critical, >1 supercritical (upstream control)
formulas.note: √(gy) is the shallow-water wave speed, which is why Fr = 1 divides the two control regimes.

formulas.label: Hydraulic jump — sequent depths
formulas.expression: y₂/y₁ = ½(√(1 + 8Fr₁²) − 1) ;   E_L = (y₂ − y₁)³/(4y₁y₂) ;   length ≈ 5–7 y₂
formulas.note: SEQUENT depths (momentum), not ALTERNATE depths (energy). Design for Fr₁ = 4.5–9.0.

formulas.label: Dynamic equation of gradually varied flow
formulas.note: dy/dx → ∞ as Fr → 1, which is why the transition through critical depth is abrupt.

formulas.label: Channel classification
formulas.expression: Mild: y_n > y_c.   Steep: y_n < y_c.
formulas.note: Decided by comparing depths, not by the numerical slope — the same slope can be mild or steep depending on Q.

formulas.label: Weir discharge exponents
formulas.expression: Rectangular Q ∝ H^{3/2} ;   V-notch Q ∝ H^{5/2} ;   ogee Q = C L H^{3/2}, C ≈ 2.2
formulas.note: The V-notch is more accurate at low flows because its area shrinks with head. √H is never a weir exponent.
